extracted.intended_audience: trademark attorneys and practitioners handling ex parte appeals to the USPTO/TTAB
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on deciding whether to file and how to prosecute ex parte trademark appeals to the Trademark Trial and Appeal Board (TTAB), including procedural deadlines, evidentiary strategy, and persuasion tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only strong cases need apply (decision to appeal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given that about 70–80% of ex parte appeals result in affirmance, only relatively strong cases should be appealed; before filing, answer whether you are better off appealing and losing or not filing at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether there are acceptable alternatives (amend to §2(f), amend to Supplemental Register, enter a disclaimer, re-apply in stylized/design form, obtain a consent agreement, or a combination); consider timing (will distinctiveness or §2(d) bar disappear with time?), whether it's 'now or never' (no acceptable alternative or registration later would be too late), and whether the Examining Attorney might change course when faced with an appeal. Proceed if the Examining Attorney is clearly and obviously wrong, but recognize such cases are rare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 2: Timing is everything (almost)
rubrics_metrics.description: Know what must be filed when and what will toll deadlines; careful review of the rules is essential because of exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing and procedural compliance can determine whether an appeal is maintained or dismissed; follow the TBMP and CFR provisions carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal only from a final refusal or second refusal on same ground
rubrics_metrics.description: An appeal can only be taken from a final refusal and/or a second refusal on the same ground (TBMP 1201.05).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not file an appeal from non-final actions; check TBMP 1201.05 to confirm appealability.

rubrics_metrics.name: File notice of appeal within six months of final refusal
rubrics_metrics.description: A timely notice of appeal must be filed within six months of the final refusal (37 CFR 2.142(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Missing the six‑month deadline risks dismissal; calendar this deadline immediately upon final refusal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pay the appeal fee by the deadline
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to pay the appeal fee by the deadline for the appeal will result in dismissal of the appeal (TBMP 1202.01 and 1202.04).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure fee payment is timely and properly documented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing a request for reconsideration does not automatically toll the notice deadline
rubrics_metrics.description: Filing a request for reconsideration does not automatically toll the deadline for filing the Notice of Appeal (37 CFR 2.64; TBMP 1202.02, 1204).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume reconsideration extends the six‑month appeal window unless specific tolling rules apply; file appeal notice separately if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant's brief deadline (60 days) unless tolled or extended
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless an extension is obtained, or a request for reconsideration has been filed, the Applicant's brief is due sixty days from receipt of the notice of appeal by the PTO (37 CFR 2.142(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The TTAB will not necessarily send reminders (see In re LiveEarth Products Inc., 49 USPQ2d 1063); calendar the 60‑day deadline and plan for extensions where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely request for reconsideration tolls brief deadline
rubrics_metrics.description: Timely filing of a request for reconsideration will toll the time for filing a brief (see Live Earth and TBMP 1203.02(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reconsideration strategically when it both preserves the right to later appeal and pauses briefing obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary record must be complete at filing unless new evidence is timely submitted
rubrics_metrics.description: The evidentiary record must be complete at the time the notice of appeal is filed, unless a request for reconsideration requesting that new evidence be considered is filed with the notice of appeal or during the time frame for filing the notice (37 CFR 2.142(d)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to follow the proper procedure for adding evidence may result in exclusion (see In re Volvo Cars of N. Am., 46 USPQ2d 1455). Plan evidence gathering so the record is complete when filing notice of appeal or include a properly‑timed request for reconsideration to add evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requests for remand after the notice deadline require good cause and additional evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: If a request for remand to submit new evidence is filed after the deadline for the notice of appeal, good cause must be shown for the late submission and the request must be accompanied by the additional evidence sought to be introduced (37 CFR 2.142(d); TBMP 1207.02).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of good cause: evidence not previously available, a new attorney is representing the applicant, a new Examining Attorney took over, or the applicant and Examining Attorney agreed to remand (see In re Pennzoil Products Co., 20 USPQ2d 1753).

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve all other objections before filing appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: All other objections to the application must be resolved before the appeal is filed (37 CFR 2.142(c); TBMP 1201.04).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not file an appeal while collateral procedural issues remain outstanding; unresolved objections can complicate or defeat an appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure TTAB is the proper forum (not a Petition to the Commissioner)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure an ex parte appeal to the TTAB is the proper forum and not a Petition to the Commissioner (TBMP 1201.05).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to distinguish procedural vs substantive grounds can result in dismissal (e.g., In re Sambado & Son Inc., 45 USPQ2d 1313). Generally, TTAB hears substantive appeals under Sections 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 23 of the Lanham Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce evidence properly into the record (use official sources for third‑party registrations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Make sure that evidence is properly introduced into the record (e.g., submit copies of third‑party registrations or copies taken from the official USPTO database, rather than merely listing them in the brief or providing an unofficial search report).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases such as In re Volvo Cars, In re Hayes, and In re Broyhill discuss procedures and exceptions for making third‑party registrations of record. Rely on official copies where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond fully to all Examining Attorney requests and objections
rubrics_metrics.description: Respond fully to all objections; if an Examining Attorney asks for information on use, provide it—do not direct the Examining Attorney to search a website for evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to produce requested information may lead to denial (see In re Planalytics, Inc., 70 USPQ2d 1453), and telling the Examining Attorney to go on a 'scavenger hunt' through a website is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 3: Procedure is often as important as substance
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural compliance (timing, proper filings, evidence handling) can be as important as the substantive merits of the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand exceptions and procedural nuances in TBMP and CFR; procedural missteps can doom even strong substantive cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 4: Argument is no substitute for evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Even the most persuasive argument will have difficulty if there is no evidence to back it up; build the evidentiary record early.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess early what evidence is needed for the nature of the rejection; allow time to generate surveys, affidavits, technical exhibits, etc., as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary guidance for Section 2(d) (likelihood of confusion) issues
rubrics_metrics.description: For §2(d) disputes, put into evidence third‑party uses and registrations (using official PTO copies), affidavits/explanatory materials for technical subject matter, affidavits attesting to lack of actual confusion, evidence of different goods/channels of trade, and factual support for any DuPont factors relied upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not merely recite DuPont factors—supply evidence showing why particular factors are relevant. Use technical brochures, patents, or affidavits when Board may be unfamiliar with the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary guidance for Section 2(e) (descriptiveness/surname/functionality) issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not accept Nexis or other evidence supporting a §2(e) refusal without further investigation—examine context, number of entries (e.g., number of surnames versus population), and other contextual clues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sometimes initially persuasive search evidence is weak on closer inspection; educate the Board where the Examining Attorney has misunderstood the industry or misunderstood use of a term as descriptive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary guidance for Section 2(f) (acquired distinctiveness) issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the §2(f) record as strong as possible: multiple detailed affidavits showing advertising expenditures, sales, years of use; use variation among affidavits; unsolicited original consumer letters preferred; substantial examples of use and promotion; consider surveys where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surveys can be decisive in some cases, though not commonly used in ex parte appeals. 'More' is generally better than 'less' for §2(f) evidence, but prioritize quality over mere quantity. A perfunctory §2(f) record invites a perfunctory affirmance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary guidance for non‑traditional trademarks (trade dress, configurations, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume non‑traditional marks face higher scrutiny; focus evidence on demonstrating public recognition of the mark as a source indicator (surveys, widespread promotional use), and prioritize quality of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare the evidentiary record to meet a higher standard of scrutiny; quantity helps but quality of evidence is more important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Request for Reconsideration strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: File a Request for Reconsideration only if there's a real chance of convincing the Examining Attorney with additional arguments or evidence; otherwise use it to place new evidence into the record to prepare for appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a reconsideration is unlikely to persuade, filing one merely gives the Examining Attorney another opportunity to strengthen the refusal. Use reconsideration tactically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plead in the alternative for §2(e) cases
rubrics_metrics.description: In §2(e) cases, plead in the alternative—argue inherent distinctiveness first, but alternatively assert acquired distinctiveness under §2(f) or registrability on the Supplemental Register.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offering alternative grounds can preserve multiple avenues to registration and may increase chances of a favorable outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continue to seek resolution with Examining Attorney
rubrics_metrics.description: Throughout the appeal process, continue looking for opportunities to resolve issues with the Examining Attorney; appeals are time‑consuming for examiners as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New evidence—even if technically untimely—may be welcomed by the Examining Attorney to end the case; do not hesitate to use it, but be mindful of record rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use procedural opportunities carefully (untimely evidence may be considered if unobjected or addressed)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you try to submit evidence after appeal is filed and the Examining Attorney does not object or addresses it substantively, the evidence may be considered (TBMP 1207.03).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This tactic carries risk but can be worthwhile in some circumstances; be strategic and cautious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on strong arguments; avoid weak or unsupported points
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not waste brief and Board attention on weak arguments (e.g., claiming different channels of trade when the cited registration lacks trade restrictions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize and concentrate on arguments supported by the evidentiary record to maximize persuasive impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not base arguments on evidence not in the record
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board will not consider arguments grounded in evidence that is not in the record, and relying on such evidence can harm credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure all factual assertions are supported by admitted evidence; do not speculate or refer to outside materials unless properly made part of the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comply with Board orders and page/appendix limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not ignore the Board's rulings (e.g., attaching evidence after a denied motion to remand, filing an 'appendix' to circumvent page limits) as such conduct is harmful to the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect procedural rulings; attempting to circumvent them can lead to adverse consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain professional tone; avoid invective
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not resort to invective or name‑calling in briefs or oral argument; it will not be well received and may be harmful to your case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain professionalism and focus on reasoned legal argument and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use oral argument only when it adds beyond the brief or clarifies complex issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Oral argument is important if you can add to what's in the brief within the record or help the Board understand complicated goods or channels of trade; must be timely requested or there will be no hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request oral argument when there is substantive value in live explanation; do not rely on it to introduce new evidence outside the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall strategy: no substitute for a compelling case on the merits
rubrics_metrics.description: A compelling merits case is essential; procedural compliance and strategic planning can make the difference between success and failure even for imperfect cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine solid substantive evidence, strict procedural compliance, and smart tactical choices (reconsideration use, settlement/consent opportunities, alternative pleadings) to maximize chances of a favorable TTAB outcome.
